properties.Name: LoanRecast

Columns.Name: LoanRecastId
Columns.Description: The unique identifier of a loan recast proceeding.

Columns.Name: RecastDate
Columns.Description: The date of the loan recast.

Columns.Name: LoanAmount
Columns.Description: The amount of money that you intend on borrowing from a financial institution for the purchase of your home. Subtracting the down payment from the purchase price of the home will provide you with the loan amount.

Columns.Name: LoanToValueRatio
Columns.Description:
The loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is the original loan amount divided by the lower of the sales price or the appraised value.

The relationship between the amount of the mortgage loan and the appraised value of the property expressed as a percentage. A LTV ratio of 90 means that a borrower is borrowing 90% of the value of the property and paying 10% as a down payment. For purchases, the value of the property is assumed to be the purchase price, for refinances the value is determined by an appraisal.

Columns.Name: InitialBorrowerPaymentRate
Columns.Description: The annual interest rate used to calculate the borrower's initial cash payment.

Columns.Name: AprBaseInterestRate
Columns.Description: The actual yearly cost of credit stated to the nearest one-fourth of one percent. Any lender subject to the federal Truth-in-Lending Act must fully disclose the APR to the borrower.

Columns.Name: PaymentDiscountInterestRate
Columns.Description: In a payment discount, the lender reduces the first year's interest rate to make the mortgagor more attractive to borrowers.

Columns.Name: InterestRateCap
Columns.Description: A provision of an ARM limiting how much interest rates may increase per adjustment period.

Columns.Name: InterestRateCeiling
Columns.Description: For an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM), the maximum interest rate, as specified in the mortgage note.

Columns.Name: InterestRateFloor
Columns.Description: For an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM), the minimum interest rate, as specified in the mortgage note.

Columns.Name: InterestAccrualRate
Columns.Description: The percentage rate at which interest accrues on the mortgage. In most cases, it is also the rate used to calculate the monthly payments, although it is not used for an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) with payment change limitations.

Columns.Name: InitialInterestRate
Columns.Description: The original interest rate of the mortgage at the time of closing.

Columns.Name: RecastAmountApplied
Columns.Description: The lump sum applied to the recast to establish the new loan.

Columns.Name: LoanRecastNote
Columns.Description: A note, comment or additional information regarding the loan recast.

Columns.Name: InterestRateCapPercentage
Columns.Description: A provision of an ARM limiting how much interest rates may increase per adjustment period.

Columns.Name: LoanApr
Columns.Description:
A figure that states the total yearly cost of a mortgage as expressed by the actual rate of interest paid. The APR includes the base interest rate, points, and any other add-on loan fees and costs. 

As a result the APR is invariably higher for the rate of interest that the lender quotes for the mortgage but gives a more accurate picture of the likely cost of the loan. 

Most mortgages are not held for their full 15 or 30 year terms, so the effective annual percentage rate is higher than the quoted APR because the points and loan fees are spread out over fewer years.

Columns.Name: InterestRateCeilingPercentage
Columns.Description: For an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM), the maximum interest rate, as specified in the mortgage note.

Columns.Name: InterestRateFloorPercentage
Columns.Description: For an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM), the minimum interest rate, as specified in the mortgage note.

Columns.Name: PeriodicRateCapPercentage
Columns.Description: A limit on the amount that the interest rate can increase or decrease during any one adjustment period, regardless of how high or low the index might be.

Columns.Name: PeriodicPaymentCapAmount
Columns.Description: The limit on the amount that payments can increase or decrease during any one adjustment period for an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) where the interest rate and principal fluctuate independently of one another.

Columns.Name: LifeOfLoanCapPercentage
Columns.Description: The maximum interest rate that can be charged during the life of the loan. Also called Lifetime Cap. This value is often expressed as an increment above the initial loan rate. For example, an adjustable rate loan with an initial rate of 7.25% and a 6% lifetime cap will never adjust above a rate of 13.25% (7.25+6.0).

Columns.Name: CapEachAdjustmentPeriodPercentageCap
Columns.Description:
A set percentage amount by which an adjustable rate mortgage may adjust each adjustment period. For adjustable loans, caps are usually quoted as two numbers as in 2/6. The first number indicates how much a loan may adjust at each adjustment period while the second number indicates how much a loan may adjust over its lifetime. 
Loans like the 3/1 and 5/1 adjustable which have an initial fixed period are quoted with 3 numbers as in 3/2/6 which would mean that the first adjustment may be as much as 3%, subsequent adjustments are capped at 2% each, and the lifetime cap is 6%. 
Two-Step loans are quoted with a single cap, which is the amount by which the loan may adjust at its single adjustment date.

Columns.Name: CapSubsequentAdjustmentPeriodPercentageCap
Columns.Description:
A set percentage amount by which an adjustable rate mortgage may adjust each adjustment period. For adjustable loans, caps are usually quoted as two numbers as in 2/6. The first number indicates how much a loan may adjust at each adjustment period while the second number indicates how much a loan may adjust over its lifetime. 
Loans like the 3/1 and 5/1 adjustable which have an initial fixed period are quoted with 3 numbers as in 3/2/6 which would mean that the first adjustment may be as much as 3%, subsequent adjustments are capped at 2% each, and the lifetime cap is 6%. 
Two-Step loans are quoted with a single cap, which is the amount by which the loan may adjust at its single adjustment date.

Columns.Name: CapLifetimeAdjustmentPercentage
Columns.Description:
A set percentage amount by which an adjustable rate mortgage may adjust each adjustment period. For adjustable loans, caps are usually quoted as two numbers as in 2/6. The first number indicates how much a loan may adjust at each adjustment period while the second number indicates how much a loan may adjust over its lifetime. 
Loans like the 3/1 and 5/1 adjustable which have an initial fixed period are quoted with 3 numbers as in 3/2/6 which would mean that the first adjustment may be as much as 3%, subsequent adjustments are capped at 2% each, and the lifetime cap is 6%. 
Two-Step loans are quoted with a single cap, which is the amount by which the loan may adjust at its single adjustment date.

Columns.Name: ArmInterestRateCapPercentage
Columns.Description: A provision of an ARM limiting how much the interest rate may increase.

Columns.Name: ArmLifetimeCapPercentage
Columns.Description: The maximum interest rate on an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) that may be charged at any point over the life of the mortgage. The lifetime cap is usually expressed as a percentage increase from an initial interest rate

Columns.Name: ArmAdjustmentDate
Columns.Description: The date on which the interest rate changes for an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM).

Columns.Name: ArmMortgagePaymentCapAmount
Columns.Description: A provision of an ARM limiting how much the mortgage payments may increase.

Columns.Name: ArmChangeFrequencyMonths
Columns.Description: The frequency (in months) of payment and/or interest rate changes in an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM).

Columns.Name: PlannedClosingDate
Columns.Description:
The planned closing date.

The closing date is when final arrangements to transfer title of property as well as allocate charges and credits. The day on which the formalities of a real estate sale are concluded. 

The certificate of title, abstract, and deed are generally prepared for the closing by an attorney and this cost charged to the buyer. The buyer signs the mortgage, and closing costs are paid. The final closing merely confirms the original agreement reached in the agreement of sale.

Columns.Name: ConfirmedClosingDate
Columns.Description:
The confirmed closing date.

The closing date is when final arrangements to transfer title of property as well as allocate charges and credits. The day on which the formalities of a real estate sale are concluded. 

The certificate of title, abstract, and deed are generally prepared for the closing by an attorney and this cost charged to the buyer. The buyer signs the mortgage, and closing costs are paid. The final closing merely confirms the original agreement reached in the agreement of sale.

Columns.Name: ActualClosingDate
Columns.Description:
The actual closing date.

The closing date is when final arrangements to transfer title of property as well as allocate charges and credits. The day on which the formalities of a real estate sale are concluded. 

The certificate of title, abstract, and deed are generally prepared for the closing by an attorney and this cost charged to the buyer. The buyer signs the mortgage, and closing costs are paid. The final closing merely confirms the original agreement reached in the agreement of sale.

Columns.Name: MaturityDate
Columns.Description: The "Due Date" of a loan.

Columns.Name: AdjustmentIntervalPeriod
Columns.Description: For an adjustable rate mortgage, the time between changes in the interest rate charged. The most common adjustment intervals are one, three or five years.

Columns.Name: BalloonLoanStopDate
Columns.Description: Date on a term loan when the balloon payment is due.

Columns.Name: LenderFirmCommitmentDate
Columns.Description: A lender's agreement to provide a loan to a specific borrower on a specific property.

Columns.Name: AssumptionClause
Columns.Description: A provision in an assumable mortgage that allows a buyer to assume responsibility for the mortgage from the seller. The loan does not need to be paid in full by the original borrower upon sale or transfer of the property.

Columns.Name: AccelerationClause
Columns.Description:
The clause in a mortgage or trust deed that stipulates the entire debt is due immediately if the mortgagee defaults under the terms of the contract. 

Condition in a mortgage that may require the balance of the loan to become due immediately, if regular mortgage payments are not made or for breach of other conditions of the mortgage.

Columns.Name: ConvertibleClause
Columns.Description: A provision in some adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) that allows the borrower to change the ARM to a fixed-rate mortgage at specified time.

Columns.Name: InterestRateCapClause
Columns.Description: A provision of an adjustable rate mortgage limiting how much interest rates may increase per adjustment period.

Columns.Name: EscalatorClause
Columns.Description: A clause in a loan providing for increases in payments or interest based on pre-determined schedules or on a specific economic index, such as the consumer price index.

Columns.Name: CovenantClause
Columns.Description: A clause in a mortgage that obligates or restricts the borrower and that, if violated, can result in foreclosure.

Columns.Name: PrepaymentClause
Columns.Description: The right given to a purchaser to pay all or part of a debt prior to its maturity. The mortgagee does not have to accept any payment other than those originally agreed to.

Columns.Name: DueOnSaleProvisionClause
Columns.Description: A provision in a mortgage that allows the lender to demand repayment in full if the borrower sells the property that serves as security for the mortgage.

Columns.Name: DueOnTransferProvisionClause
Columns.Description: This terminology is usually used for second mortgages.

Columns.Name: CoinsuranceClause
Columns.Description: A provision in a hazard insurance policy that states the amount of coverage that must be maintained -- as a percentage of the total value of the property -- for the insured to collect the full amount of a loss.

Columns.Name: LockInClause
Columns.Description: Clause in a loan agreement that states that the borrower cannot repay a loan prior to a specified date.

Columns.Name: CallOptionClause
Columns.Description: A provision in the mortgage that gives the mortgagee the right to call the mortgage due and payable at the end of a specified period for whatever reason.

Columns.Name: ReconveyanceClause
Columns.Description:
Reconveyance Clause - 
The clause in a trust deed that gives the title back to the borrower when the loan is paid in full.

Columns.Name: FullRecastingIndicator
Columns.Description: Full Recasting is setting the P&I payments to the level that will fully amortize the loan's outstanding balance over the remaining term using the fully indexed accrual rate at the recasting point.

Columns.Name: LoanRecastReasonId
Columns.Description: The unique identifier of a Mortgage Loan recast Reason.

Columns.Name: CustomerAccountId
Columns.Description: The unique identifier of a Customer Account.

Columns.Name: RecastAsCustomerAccountId
Columns.Description: The unique identifier of a Customer Account.

Properties.Description:
To redesign an existing loan balance into a new loan for the same period or longer, to reduce payments and help a distressed borrower. 

Recast, in this context, is a fancy way of saying recalculate. An even more fancy way of saying recalculate is to say reamortize. No matter how you say it, they all mean the same thing.

When a mortgage is recast, the lender works out a new amortization schedule, usually with the same interest rate, after the borrower has made a large payment on the loan to pay down the principal balance. Typically, this type of recasting can only occur once during the life of a loan.

Though it is possible for recasting to occur after someone comes into a large sum of money and pays down their home mortgage, it most frequently occurs when a borrower is in financial distress and needs to refinance to lower monthly payments.
